newsitem.title: USA: Clinton offers to compromise on tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Clinton offers to compromise on tax cuts.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Monday offered to compromise with Congress on tax cuts, proposing a broad capital gains tax break and a revised tax credit for children as well as an increase in the tax on cigarettes.
In making the announcement, Clinton said, "America's families deserve a tax cut and they deserve one that reflects their values."

The White House said his plan would provide a net $85 billion tax cut in five years with 67 percent of the tax cut going to families in the middle 60 percent of income brackets. The administration has criticised tax cuts developed by Republicans in Congress as being too generous to the wealthy.
The Republican-controlled House of Representatives and Senate each approved last week detailed legislation that would give Americans their first major tax cut in 16 years.

But Democrat Clinton has expressed reservations about much of the Republican plan and the announcement on Monday was designed to set out his negotiating position with Congress, which will finalise its plan after the July 4 holiday.
Details of the president's tax proposal are as follows:
-- A 30 percent exclusion on long-term capital gains taxes for investments held over one year. The tax rate would not be indexed for inflation.
-- A 20 cent per pack increase in the tobacco tax to be put in a separate trust fund used to expand health coverage for children.
-- Exclusion of $900,000 from tax on family farm and family business estates.
-- $500,000 exclusion for capital gains on home sales for a couple, $250,000 for single filers.
-- New 50 percent tax credit on the first $10,000 of wages to help welfare recipients return to work.

-- Child tax credit of $400 in 1998, $500 in 1999 and thereafter. Covers children under 17 through 2002 and under 19 thereafter. Phased out for families making $60,000-$75,000 until 2000 and then $80,000-$100,000 thereafter. Partially refundable to working families against payroll taxes.
-- Two-year HOPE scholarships with a maximum credit of $1,500 a year beginning in 1998.

-- 20 percent tuition tax credit for third and fourth year students, graduate students and working people who return for -- Penalty-free withdrawals from Individual Retirement Accounts to pay for higher education and first-home pruchase.
-- New Kidsave accounts which parents can contribute up to $1,000 a year for education, first-home purchase or retirement.
-- Tax deduction of up to $2,500 a year of interest on student loans.
-- Tax incentives for donations of computer equipment to schools.
-- Tax incentives for environmental cleanup allowing full deduction immediately of costs, also called "Brownfields" clean up.
-- Puerto Rico tax credit extended indefinitely.
-- Research and Experimentation credit extended through the end of 1998.
-- Increased exclusion from tax to 75 percent for equity investments of at least $20 million in small businesses held at least five years. The size of eligible firms would be doubled to $100 million.
-- Expanded empowerment zones as contained in the president's 1998 budget.
-- Tax incentives to hire residents of Washington D.C., issuance of additional tax-exempt debt to help businesses in the district and a new credit allocated to a new economic development corporation.
